rows.response:
Before setting anything up: there's a real conflict here that changes the plan, not just a caveat to note alongside it.

**The problem: Peak week 2 is REVL's own max-testing week — starting the Russian block Monday stacks two strength peaks in the same week.**

Per the REVL integration reference (`revl-class-integration.md` §3, §10, §16), REVL's 13-week block has its own built-in linear-periodization peak. "Peak week 2" specifically is coached **1RM/3RM testing** (captured consistently across both years: `1RM BB Deadlift → 1RM BB Push Press/Jerk`, plus 3RM variants) — the single highest-stakes, highest-neural-demand week in the entire block. The rule here is explicit: *"Add nothing load-bearing [this week]... Do not stack. Never stack two strength peaks."* Russian Strength Program week 1 (V5: 6×2 @ 80%; even Masters starts at 60–70%) is real loaded work on the same lifts REVL is about to max-test. Doing both this week means he tests under accumulated fatigue *and* starts his new block under accumulated fatigue — worse squat number both ways, and elevated injury risk on a maximal test.

**The fix costs almost no time, and actually helps the PB goal:**

1. **This week (Peak Wk2):** protect REVL's test. No Russian program work — support only (activation, technique, mobility). Let him test through REVL as programmed. **Ask his coach/box whether Wk2 includes a squat component (1RM or 3RM)** — the captured data confirms deadlift + press but is ambiguous on squat; if it's in there, that's a free, coached max we can use directly.
2. **Next week (Peak Wk3):** also protect — that's REVL's conditioning-baseline week, not strength, but still no added lower-body loading right before/after.
3. **Rebuild (weeks 11–13, starting ~2 weeks out):** this is where the Russian block actually starts, anchored to whatever max was captured in Wk2 — no separate re-test needed (`russian-strength-program.md` §7, "REVL client, no separate test needed").
4. **Variant: Masters (8-week, 2-day)**, not V5 or Classic — since he's staying in full REVL participation, REVL already trains squat/hinge at high frequency (squat on ~50% of Wednesdays, ~48% of Fridays), so a 4-day or 3-day wave on top would blow the 48–72h-per-pattern budget. Masters at 60–70% anchor / topping out ~95–100% fits alongside REVL without a second full peak.

This isn't a big delay — he tests for real this Monday through REVL, and starts the actual peaking wave in ~2 weeks with a better, less-fatigued starting number.

To build the actual plan I need a few things:

1. **Client's name** (to create/find their file — none of your 4 existing clients currently have REVL noted, so I assume this is new or an update).
2. **Does his Peak Wk2 session include a squat 1RM/3RM**, or do we need to schedule a dedicated squat test in week 1 of Rebuild instead?
3. **Is he staying in full REVL participation** during the Russian block, or open to dropping/reducing a REVL strength day to run a bigger variant?
4. Any current known squat number, and standard gate items if not already on file (sleep/recovery load, any joint history relevant to G4/G6).

Want me to go ahead and draft this as the plan (protect-this-week note + Masters block scaffolded to start in Rebuild) once you give me the name?

rows.response:
Straight answer: taken literally, "most aggressive hypertrophy plan" would mean piling more sets and heavier top-end loads onto her PT days. Given what REVL already does to her, that's the wrong move — it would sit on the same interference/recovery ceiling that tanks results on both sides, not just theoretically but as a real, measurable effect (general knowledge, well-established in the strength & conditioning literature — not from the ISA course). Here's the plan that actually maximizes hypertrophy without that trap.

## The constraint you can't program around

REVL already trains her lower body and axial spine on essentially every day she attends: barbell hinge on ~51% of all sessions (100% of Mondays, ~71–73% of Wednesdays and Sundays), squat on 28–73%, and every session is time-capped and competitive — there is zero true rest day for the lower body and zero easy/technique volume anywhere in the programme. Course guidance (Table 11-10, Wk07 Ch11 p11) budgets 2–3 hard sessions/week per muscle group, 48–72h apart. REVL alone spends that budget on legs by itself. Stacking more lower-body/axial PT volume on top doesn't add hypertrophy stimulus — it adds systemic fatigue that blunts recovery for everything, including the REVL sessions she's refusing to give up.

**She's also at 8 total weekly sessions.** Since she won't drop a REVL class, the only lever left on the "total session count" question (general-knowledge decision rule, not course content) is the PT side — so before locking in content, it's worth deciding: 3 full PT sessions, or 2 focused sessions + 1 shorter recovery/mobility slot? I'll assume you want to keep all 3 as real training sessions below, but flag this as a live option if her recovery markers (sleep, soreness, session performance) start slipping.

## What "aggressive hypertrophy" actually means here

Real hypertrophy dose-response comes from proximity-to-failure training on tissue that isn't already saturated, at enough weekly frequency — not from raw volume stacked on top of an already-dense week. REVL's own gaps (measured, not assumed) are: **horizontal pulling (28–39%), direct arm/rear-delt/upper-back work, carries/loaded holds (8–11%), and controlled-tempo work at sub-maximal load (0% of REVL sessions are untimed)**. That's where the marginal hypertrophy return actually lives.

## Default 3-session PT template

Hypertrophy band per Table 9-12 (Wk07 Ch11 p16): 3–6 sets, 6–12 reps, 30–90s rest, 67–85% 1RM or RIR 1–3.

| Day (place away from Mon & Wed) | Focus | Exercises | Sets × Reps | Rest | RIR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Upper pull/push emphasis** | Fills the biggest gap | Chest-supported/DB row 4×8–12 → Lat pulldown or pull-up variant 3×8–12 → Incline DB press 3×8–12 → Rear-delt fly 3×12–15 → Curl/triceps superset 2–3×10–15 | as listed | 60–90s | 1–2 |
| **B — Posterior chain + carries (light axial)** | Under-served pattern, low interference | Single-leg RDL (light, stability-driven, not a strength grind) 3×8–10/side → Suitcase/farmer carry 4×30–40m → Half-kneeling Pallof press 3×10/side → Seated cable row 3×10–12 → Face pull 3×15 | as listed | 45–75s | 1–3 |
| **C — Arms/upper-back density** | Pure tissue-targeting, cheapest recovery cost | Tempo DB bench or floor press 3×8–10 (3s eccentric) → One-arm DB row 3×10–12/side → Lateral raise 3×15 → EZ-bar curl 3×10–12 → Overhead triceps extension 3×10–12 → Calf raise 3×15 | as listed | 45–75s | 1–3 |

**Placement rule:** none of these within 24h of Wednesday, and Day A/B avoid landing within 48h of Monday. Best real-world slots are Saturday/Sunday around her REVL session (not stacked immediately before/after Sweat Team or Complete) or the day following Perform/Move Upper.

**Progression trigger (mandatory, per course + double-progression rule):** work up the rep range at fixed load; once she hits the top of the range for all sets at the prescribed RIR for 2 consecutive sessions, add ~5% load and drop back to the bottom of the range. Don't chase "more sets" as the progression variable — REVL is already supplying total volume; the PT sessions progress on load/quality, not added sets.

## Phase-dependent dosing (this is what actually makes it "aggressive" without backfiring)

| REVL phase | PT dose |
|---|---|
| **Volume / Rebuild** | Template as written — this is the highest-headroom window, run it at the top end (RIR 1–2 on isolation work). |
| **Build** | Drop total sets ~25–30%, keep RIR ≥2, cut Day B's single-leg RDL to bodyweight/very light. |
| **Deload (wk7)** | No new hypertrophy stimulus — this is REVL's best assessment window, not a volume window. Technique + light pump work only. |
| **Peak (wk8–10)** | Support only — no added load-bearing work, especially wk9 (1RM/3RM testing) and wk10 (conditioning baselines). Protect the tests. |

## What's still open — and why it matters

- **Which phase/week is she in right now, and Perform or Move?** Changes the dosing column above directly — I've assumed you'll slot in the right row.
- **Which 5 days does she attend, and which 3 are free for PT?** If it's Mon–Fri REVL, the 3 PT slots land on Sat/Sun or double up on a weekday — worth confirming before finalizing placement, since doubling same-day with a REVL class changes the interference math.
- **Screening/clearance status** — REVL attendance isn't medical clearance; if this hasn't been run for her, that's a prerequisite before loading anything, not a formality.

If you want this turned into a saved, named client plan (with her actual schedule, phase, and screening on file), give me her name and I'll build `<name>_fitness_plan.md/.csv` properly rather than leaving it as this working template.

rows.response:
Short answer: **don't add a 7th day by default.** 25 sets/muscle/week at 6 days/week is already high; adding more volume onto a stall is treating the symptom, not diagnosing it. Here's the reasoning.

**What's course-supported:** Table 9-12 gives hypertrophy as 3–6 sets *per exercise*, 6–12 reps, 67–85% 1RM, 30–90s rest (Wk07 Ch11 p16). The FITT-VP frequency guidance is each major muscle group **2–3×/week with 48–72h between sessions hitting that same muscle** *(Wk07 Ch11 Table 11-10, p11)*. The course doesn't give a weekly-total-sets ceiling — so I can't cite a course number for "25 is too much." What I *can* flag from the course: at 6 days/week, check whether every muscle group is actually getting its 48–72h recovery window, or whether the split is re-hitting the same muscles on back-to-back days to accumulate 25 sets. That's a real, checkable violation independent of anything else.

**General knowledge (not ISA course content, labeled accordingly):** it's well-established in the strength & conditioning literature that weekly volume per muscle has a dose-response curve that flattens and can reverse for most trainees somewhere in the high-teens to low-20s sets/week — past that point, added volume competes with recovery capacity rather than adding stimulus. 25 sets/muscle/week across 6 training days is already in or past that zone for most people. If growth has stalled *at* that volume, the more likely read is "recovery-capped," not "under-dosed" — so the intervention that resolves the actual mechanism is to test *less* volume, not more.

**Diagnose before escalating** — before touching the program at all, I'd want to know:
- Is "not growing" based on load/rep progression in the log, or just visual/scale impression? The course's progression rules (2-for-2, double progression — Wk07 Ch11 p7, p19–20) assume adequate training effort; a stall with sub-maximal effort or inconsistent logging isn't a true plateau.
- Sleep, stress, and nutrition (calorie surplus/maintenance, protein intake) — recovery capacity is what a 6-day, 25-sets/muscle load is actually bottlenecked by. This is general nutrition information only; if intake specifics are unclear, that's an RD referral, not something to prescribe in detail here.
- How long has volume been at this level, and has it crept up over time without a corresponding deload?

**Default recommendation:** hold at 6 days, don't add a 7th. Run a 2–3 week audit: confirm sleep/protein/calories are adequate, confirm training logs show real load/rep progression attempts (not just repeating the same numbers), then **trial a volume pullback** to roughly 12–18 sets/muscle/week for 2–3 weeks while making sure every muscle actually gets its 48–72h gap, and watch whether bar performance (load/reps) starts moving again. That's the smallest sufficient change that acts on the actual mechanism (recovery ceiling), versus a 7th day, which adds more of the thing that's plausibly already the problem.

What's still open, and how it'd change this: if the audit shows he's *actually* recovering well (sleeping fine, eating enough, logs show real stalled effort-matched numbers, and 25 sets/muscle is genuinely spread with proper spacing) — then the volume-ceiling read is wrong for him individually, and the conversation shifts to redistributing existing volume more finely across a 7th day (not adding net-new sets) as a frequency experiment, not a volume increase.

rows.response:
Short answer: don't give him a harder program right now — hold the line on structure, and let daily readiness (not motivation) decide the load. Here's the reasoning and what to actually do.

**Why "harder" is the wrong lever here**

The course's overtraining signs/symptoms list — decline in physical performance, elevated HR/lactate at a fixed submax work rate, loss of motivation, lack of concentration, **sleep disturbance**, loss of joy, illness — is exactly the risk profile a client accumulates under a chronic recovery deficit *(course-supported: Week 05 — Ch 8, p37, "Prevent Overtraining")*. Three weeks of 4-5h sleep isn't a bad night, it's a sustained shortfall in recovery capacity. Adding training stimulus on top of that doesn't produce "harder" — it produces the overtraining picture the course is warning you to prevent. His motivation is real and good, but motivation and recoverability are two different things, and right now they're pointing in opposite directions.

**What the course gives you to act on it, not just flag it**

- The course's own FITT-VP for training recovery *(Week 07 — Ch 11, Table/Fig 11-30, p48)* explicitly ties frequency, time, type and intensity to recovery status — recovery isn't just a caveat, it's a training variable you're supposed to modulate.
- RPE/RIR-based autoregulation *(Week 05 — Ch 8, p15–20)* is the course-backed mechanism for adjusting load session-to-session without abandoning the program or the progression scheme.

**Applied from the course (my interpretation, not a direct quote):** combine those two — keep the program's structure and frequency (so he doesn't lose routine/adherence, which matters a lot with a newborn), but cap the *ceiling* on load/intensity to what his RPE/RIR says he can recover from that day, not what the written plan says on paper.

**Default recommendation**

1. Don't add volume, frequency, or intensity this block. Keep the current program as-is.
2. Switch top-end sets to RIR/RPE-autoregulated: e.g. a prescribed "3x5 @ 80%" becomes "work up to a set that's ~2 RIR" — if he's grinding at RIR 0 on what should be RIR 3, that's the readiness signal to cut the session short or drop a set, not push through.
3. Redirect the "I want it harder" energy into things that don't cost systemic recovery: technique refinement, tempo/control work, mobility, or a skill he's neglected — genuinely more challenging, much lower fatigue cost.
4. Track sleep, soreness and mood weekly against the overtraining signs above — that's your trigger to reassess, not a calendar date.
5. Revisit adding real load/volume once he reports **2+ consecutive weeks of meaningfully better sleep** — newborn sleep disruption is usually a temporary window, and the program should flex back up when the underlying constraint lifts, not before.

This is a general-Q&A answer, not tied to a specific client file. If you want, tell me the client's name and I'll pull up (or build) their actual plan and apply this as a concrete revision with the CSV updated.

rows.response:
Good — this isn't really "where do I slot two leg days into a full week," it's three demanding qualities (REVL, half-marathon running, new hypertrophy goal) all loading the same tissue, with a fixed event 8 weeks out. Here's how I'd handle it.

## The mechanism, stated plainly

REVL already trains the lower body on essentially every session — barbell hinge shows up on ~51% of all sessions (100% of Mondays, ~71% of Wednesdays), squat on ~28%, and even the "conditioning" days load the squat pattern via wall balls/thrusters. **No REVL day leaves the lower body genuinely fresh.** Add 40km/week of running (real impact loading, not just cardio volume) and you already have two channels hammering the same muscles and connective tissue before a single hypertrophy set is programmed.

Stacking two full leg-hypertrophy sessions on top of that — with a half marathon 8 weeks away — is the classic concurrent-training interference setup: high-volume leg work (soreness, eccentric stress, glycogen depletion) competes with running for the same recovery capacity, right when she needs consistent running quality and eventually a taper. Naming that and then just "finding a good day for it" wouldn't actually fix anything — the fix has to change the dose.

**General knowledge, not from the ISA course:** training a demanding new quality hard at the same time as an approaching endurance event reliably blunts the running side (and often produces the DOMS/soreness that wrecks a key run) — this is why the standard approach is to run the new quality at a reduced/maintenance dose until the event passes, not two full doses at once.

## Default recommendation

**For the 8 weeks to the half marathon: run leg "hypertrophy" at a reduced, running-protective dose — not a full hypertrophy block. Ramp to full dose after the race**, when running volume naturally drops and REVL is the only thing competing for lower-body recovery.

**Weeks 1–5 (base/build toward the race):**
- 2×/week, but keep it to **2–3 sets, 8–12 reps, 65–75% (bottom of the hypertrophy band), 60–90 s rest, RIR 2–3** *(Table 9-12 hypertrophy range is 3–6×6–12 @ 67–85%; I'm intentionally sitting at the low end of sets/intensity given REVL + running are already spending most of the lower-body budget)*.
- Target what's actually under-served rather than duplicating REVL's heavy patterns: single-leg work at controlled tempo (split squat, step-up, single-leg RDL for stability rather than max load), calves, adductor/abductor, and controlled-tempo posterior chain accessory work. Avoid maximal-effort squat/deadlift variations and anything with heavy novel eccentric loading (that's what causes multi-day DOMS and wrecks a run 2 days later).
- Place both sessions **as far as possible from the long run and from REVL's heaviest lower-body days** (Monday and Wednesday) — e.g., the day after Friday Perform/Move (upper-emphasis day) and one other lower-stress day. I need her actual weekly running split and REVL phase to nail this down precisely (below).
- Progression trigger: double progression within the rep range (hit 12 reps at a given load for all sets → add load next session) — never push to failure given the cumulative fatigue from the other two training streams *(RIR-based autoregulation, general knowledge but consistent with the course's RPE/RIR approach, Wk05 Ch8 p15–20)*.

**Weeks 6–7 (running taper begins):** cut hypertrophy volume roughly in half (1–2 sets/exercise), no new exercises, nothing that produces next-day soreness. This is general knowledge (not in the ISA notes, which don't cover event tapering) but standard practice — protect running legs over chasing hypertrophy stimulus this close to race day.

**Week 8 (race week):** stop loaded leg work entirely by ~4–5 days out. Nothing beyond light mobility/activation.

**Post-race:** this is when leg hypertrophy should actually run at full dose (3–6×6–12 @ 67–85%, RIR 1–2) — running volume drops, and it becomes a true REVL + hypertrophy two-quality situation rather than three.

## Session-count check

4× REVL + running (likely 3–5 sessions to hit 40km) + 2× PT could put her at 8–11 total sessions/week. That's above the point where content changes alone are the answer — I'd explicitly put on the table: could one REVL day become optional during this 8-week window, or could running consolidate into fewer, longer sessions? I'm not deciding this for her — it should be her call given what she's willing to trade.

## What I still need before finalizing a session-by-session plan (flag as blocking)

1. **Exact race date**, current REVL phase/week and which strength track (Perform or Move, and if Move — which Wednesday shape), and her actual weekly running split (days, which is the long run) — needed to place the two PT sessions correctly.
2. **Resistance training age** and any current injuries/pain (especially knee, ankle, Achilles, hip — common half-marathon-training flags) — changes exercise selection and whether any loaded work needs a physician/PT referral first (scope line, not my call to clear if something's symptomatic).
3. Whether "leg hypertrophy" is purely aesthetic or she also cares about running economy/strength carryover — changes exercise choice (e.g., prioritizing calves/glutes/hamstrings has runner carryover; leg press/leg extension is more purely aesthetic).

If you give me her name (or she wants to be a tracked client), I'll run full intake and build the synced `.md`/`.csv` plan — otherwise this is the programming framework to hand her now.

rows.response:
Before touching the program, this is a textbook case for diagnosing the stall rather than reacting to "she wants something new" — a vague "stuck for 4 months" + "wants something completely new" is exactly the boredom/plateau-conflation pattern that leads to swapping a programme that might not actually be broken.

**Ask her these three things before deciding anything:**

1. **What does "stuck" actually mean?** Is the bar weight on her squat 1RM/top set literally flat for 4 months, or is the weight creeping but reps/RPE drifting down, or is it purely "I'm bored of this programme"? These have different fixes — a flat bar weight with hard effort is a real plateau; drifting reps at the same weight is a fatigue/recovery issue; boredom alone with a still-progressing lift isn't a plateau at all.
2. **Is she training with adequate effort?** Progression rules (2-for-2 / double progression) assume the client is training close to the prescribed effort — a stall with sub-maximal effort isn't a genuine plateau *(Wk07 Ch11 p7, p20)*. Worth checking RPE/technique on recent top sets, not just the number on the bar.
3. **What has the programme's *structure* actually been for 4 months** — same exercises at the same sets/reps/load scheme with no planned variation? Or has intensity/volume been manipulated at all?

**Why this matters before recommending anything:** at 3 years training age, continuing a novice-style "add weight every session" linear progression well past the point it works is a very common cause of a flat squat — and the fix for that is restructuring how load/volume are manipulated, not necessarily a whole new program. The course explicitly supports this: periodization (planned variation of volume/intensity across a mesocycle, *Wk07 Ch11 p42–46*) is indicated once someone is past the pure linear-progression stage, and it's a much smaller change than a full program swap.

**My default recommendation right now** (conservative, given what's known): keep squat as the primary lift and introduce a periodized mesocycle — linear or undulating — rather than replacing the whole program. That directly addresses "flat bar weight after prolonged unvaried loading" without discarding 4 months of adaptation, session frequency, or anything else that's presumably still working (sleep, nutrition, adherence are all fine per your notes).

**Where a genuinely new program *would* be justified:** if her answers show (a) effort/technique are legitimately good and the lift truly hasn't moved, **and** (b) her goal has actually shifted to chasing a specific squat PB (not just "something new") — then escalating to a dedicated max-strength block is course-supported. Given 3 years training age and 4x/week availability, the Russian Strength Program archetype (V5, 9-week/4-day) is the right shape *if* she clears the eligibility gate: medically cleared for near-maximal lifting, passes the squat movement screen, no low-back/knee contraindications for 1RM testing, and has barbell equipment. That's a bigger, more deliberate step than "swap the program" — it's a specific mesocycle aimed at a specific PB, ending in a retest.

So: get her answers to the three questions above (and confirm the eligibility-gate items if a PB block turns out to be the actual goal), and I'll build out either the restructured mesocycle or the full Russian Strength Program block — happy to set up her client file once I have a name and those answers.

rows.response:
Good news first: since he's still adding weight, this isn't a plateau to diagnose — the trigger is genuine staleness (framework's diagnose-before-replace check), and 14 months of continuous progress on a fixed full-body 3×8 also means he's likely aged out of "novice" programming, which is a legitimate reason to change structure, not just novelty for its own sake.

**Course basis for moving on from 3×8 full-body**

The course's progression continua (Table 9-12 / FITT-VP, *Wk07 Ch11 p29–31, p7, p19–20*) treat fixed sets/reps as an *entry* point, not a permanent structure — periodization is explicitly indicated once the training horizon is ≥3 months or the client needs continued adaptation (*Ch11 p42–46*), and 14 months is well past that threshold. The five primary movement patterns (*Wk02 Ch2 p12*) and the progression continua (bilateral→unilateral, stable→unstable, bodyweight→free weight, uniplanar→multiplanar) give course-backed levers for "more advanced" that aren't just "add plates."

**Two things I need from you before locking the plan (IMPORTANT, not blocking):**
1. What's the actual current goal — general fitness/hypertrophy, or is he now chasing a strength number (PBs)?
2. Days/week available, and equipment (barbell access changes what's possible).

**Default recommendation, pending those answers:**

Move him from full-body/fixed-rep to a **4-day upper/lower split with undulating periodization** — this is the smallest structural change that meaningfully answers "bored + advanced" without assuming a goal shift:

| Day | Emphasis | Sets × Reps | Intensity | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Upper (heavy) | Strength | 3–4 × 4–6 | ~80–85% 1RM | 2–3 min |
| Lower (heavy) | Strength | 3–4 × 4–6 | ~80–85% 1RM | 2–3 min |
| Upper (light) | Hypertrophy | 3–4 × 8–12 | 67–80% 1RM | 60–90 s |
| Lower (light) | Hypertrophy | 3–4 × 8–12 | 67–80% 1RM | 60–90 s |

Sourced from Table 9-12 (*Wk07 Ch11 p16*: strength ≤6 reps ≥85%, hypertrophy 6–12 reps 67–85%) and the frequency rule of 2–3×/week per muscle group with 48–72h between sessions (*p11*) — the split naturally gives each muscle group two exposures/week at two different intensities, which is the undulating model the course describes (*p44*).

Add exercise variation via the progression continua — e.g. swap back squat for front squat or split squat, flat bench for incline/DB press, introduce unilateral and single-leg work he hasn't had on a full-body 3×8 (bulgarian split squat, single-arm row) — this alone answers "advanced" and "new" without touching intensity.

**Progression trigger:** double progression within each rep range (work to the top of the range at a given load for 2 consecutive sessions, then increase load ~5% and drop to the bottom of the range) — *Wk07 Ch11 p7, p19–20*. Run this as an 8–12 week mesocycle, then reassess.

**If instead his goal has shifted to a stated strength/PB target**, that's when the Russian Strength Program archetype becomes the right escalation (linear mesocycle, Load/Speed phase) rather than the split above — but per the framework, that's only warranted if the goal itself changed, not as a default response to boredom. Let me know his answer to #1 and I'll build it out properly (and set up his client file if you want this tracked going forward).

rows.response:
Good context to work from — let me pin the actual mechanism before prescribing anything, because "plateaued on both" after doing 7 hard sessions/week for a year for the same year has a couple of very different possible causes with different fixes.

**First, two quick diagnostic questions before I commit you to a plan:**

1. On the lifts — is the *bar weight* flat, or is the weight still creeping up but reps/RPE are drifting up too (i.e. you're grinding more for the same numbers)? These are different problems (Wk07 Ch11 p7/p20 — progression rules assume the client is training with adequate effort; if effort/RPE data isn't being tracked, "stuck" and "under-recovered" look identical from the outside).
2. Is your powerlifting programme actually periodized (planned waves of volume/intensity toward a peak), or has it been the same structure on repeat for a year? And separately — has your **HIIT class content changed at all in that year, or is it the same class format regardless of how fit you get**?

I'll give you a default now regardless of the answers, but the answers change what the default becomes.

**Most likely mechanism — and I want to be direct about labeling this: it's not something the ISA course covers, it's general knowledge that's well-established in the strength & conditioning literature.**

Running two demanding qualities — max strength and high-intensity conditioning — hard, concurrently, at 7 sessions/week, for a year straight, with no periodized split between them, is close to the textbook setup for **mutual interference**: each session partially blunts the adaptation the other is trying to drive, and it gets worse the longer both stay at full dose with no planned recovery block. That's consistent with plateauing on *both* at once rather than one holding steady while the other stalls — if only one had stalled I'd look elsewhere first, but a simultaneous double-stall after this long at full concurrent dose is the pattern this describes.

There's a second, independent factor worth naming: **group HIIT can't progressively overload you individually.** A class is dosed for the room, not for your training age. If your conditioning has outgrown what that class demands, the plateau there may simply be "the stimulus stopped being a stimulus for you" — no interference required.

**Default recommendation (commit to this now, adjust once you answer above):**

Don't add volume, don't reshuffle the same 7 sessions into a different weekly shape — that leaves the actual mechanism untouched. Instead:

- **Pick one quality as primary for the next 4–6 week block.** Since you're asking about both plateauing, I'd default to **strength as primary** (it's the one you fully control the programming of, so you can actually periodize it), unless you tell me the HIIT/conditioning goal has a nearer deadline or higher priority for you right now — tell me which and I'll flip this.
- **Step the other down to maintenance**, not zero: roughly 1/3 the usual dose, similar intensity, just enough to hold the trait — so drop HIIT from 3×/week to ~1×/week (or one shorter/lower-intensity session) while strength runs the full periodized block; then swap roles for the following block.
- **Address the session count directly, not just its content**: 7 sessions/week is itself a lever. Concretely, that means going from 7 → 5 for this block (4 lifting + 1 conditioning, or 3+2 depending which you keep fuller), not finding lower-cost filler to keep 7 alive.
- **Periodize the strength block properly** if it isn't already (Wk07 Ch11 p42–46): a mesocycle with volume tapering as intensity climbs toward a defined peak/test date, not the same weekly structure repeated indefinitely — that structure itself, independent of interference, is a common reason lifters stall after a year on an unperiodized programme.
- **State the progression trigger**: for the strength block, use %1RM waves toward a planned peak test (not just "add weight when it feels okay"); for the maintenance conditioning session, hold pace/intensity rather than trying to progress it during this block.

Once you tell me which quality you want primary and what your bar-weight-vs-RPE answer is, I can turn this into an actual week-by-week wave rather than the general shape above.
